turns.note: I am testing a seven-column sequence that recovers C3, C4, C5 and C6 blends plus heptane, octane and nonane, using moderate separation severity to establish purity and cost tradeoffs.

The measured moderate-severity columns all converge but leave every outlet below its 95% sales threshold. I am keeping the same seven-column C5/C6-paraffin/naph-thene/heptane/octane/nonane topology and sharply increasing separation severity to establish a revenue-generating baseline.

I am using the measured convergent C3/C5 baseline, deleting the heavy branch that generated no revenue, and sharpening only the small C3/C4 splitter to recover the valuable C4 blend and propane left in its bottoms.

Copy the measured 1.088-reward flowsheet and add three direct product-recovery splits: propane/C4, heptane/octane, and octane/nonane. These streams already have concentrated valuable components, so the added sales should outweigh moderate column costs.

I am starting from the measured 1.088 six-column design and targeting the largest recoverable losses: C4/propane, heptane/octane, and octane/nonane. The stronger T split should keep C5 out of the C4 product; sharper heavy cuts should convert currently worthless streams into sales.
Restore the measured convergent light-end column; the current 60-stage/4-reflux/5-boil-up setting failed and blocked all light-product recovery.

Interpretation: the largest remaining upside is the unsold C6 pool; a much sharper paraffin/naphthene cut should monetize both blends. I am also reducing C5 leakage into the C4 branch and shifting the C7/C8 column toward an octane-rich bottoms product.

The measured TB stream is only 93% C5 and TTBB only 86% C4, so I am increasing boil-up in their upstream columns to push C4 overhead and unlock both blend sales. BBT currently adds $38.4M/yr cost with no saleable outlet, so I am removing it; this also avoids its component-balance validation failure.

The measured zero-value BTB stream contains enough C6 paraffins and naphthenes for two saleable blends, while BBT contains most of the heptane. I am adding a paraffin/naphthene split and a two-step cyclohexane removal/heptane recovery sequence.

I am sharpening the C4/C5 cut to recover a saleable C4 blend, making the C6 paraffin/naphthene split directly at BT, and adding the missing cyclohexane/heptane split. I am also tightening the residual C7/C8 column, whose current bottoms discard valuable heptane and octane.

Two currently worthless heavy streams contain large saleable pools. I am testing a severe n-hexane/MCP cut on BTB and a conventional C7/C8 split on BBTBB; the retrieved evidence supports sharper downstream cuts, while the settings here are new hypotheses.

The measured zero-value pools still contain saleable C3/C4/C5, cyclohexane, heptane and octane. I will sharpen the C3/C4 cut, push the difficult hexane/naphthene column to its severity limit, and add small final splits on the two mixed heavy leaves.

The max-severity C6 cut still leaves 18% hexane in the naphthene bottoms. I am testing a much lower column pressure to increase relative volatility and recover the high-value C6 naphthene blend without adding equipment.

I interpret the measured 97% octane and nonane products as near-premium opportunities, while TTB has zero measured sales and can be removed for an immediate cost saving. I am also testing recovery of the unsold C6 naphthene and cyclohexane-rich pools.

The TTB column has two zero-value outlets, so I am removing it. I am also testing sharper heavy-end and cyclohexane splits: the measured octane and nonane products are only 97% pure, and reaching 99% would activate substantial premiums.

Measured: TTB, BTBB, BBTTTT and BBTBBTB are unsold, while BBBT is 97% octane. Interpretation: targeted polishing splits should recover C3/C4/C5, naphthenes, cyclohexane and premium octane with modest added cost.

The measured BBBT stream is already 97% octane, so selling it directly should exceed the value of its single premium child while eliminating a column. I am also removing a zero-revenue cyclohexane splitter and testing a C4-overhead/C5-bottoms cut on TTB to monetize both currently unsold light ends.

I am targeting measured, high-value losses: drive residual propane and butane upward in TTB to expose C4/C5 blends, push the 97% octane stream to premium grade, and recover heptane/cyclohexane from two small unsold outlets. The heavier settings are localized to avoid disturbing the main C6 split.
Return to the measured best-valid design before making further cost-reduction changes; the current variant is about $91M/yr less profitable.

I expect two small finishing columns to turn the unsold C3/C4 and C4/C5 pools into saleable blends. I am also testing whether lower pressure makes the difficult hexane/naphthene cut sharp enough to sell BTB bottoms directly and eliminate BTBB.

The measured BT split leaves 37 mol/s hexane contaminating an otherwise saleable C6 naphthene pool; higher boil-up should move that hexane into the already-saleable paraffin tops. I am also sharpening the small cyclohexane/heptane split, whose current tops are only 76% cyclohexane.

Measured: five streams are unsold despite containing saleable naphthenes, cyclohexane, C4/C5 material, propane, and heptane. Interpretation: sharper local splits should recover that value without disturbing the converged upstream flowsheet; the new TTBTT column also tests recovery of its propane/isobutane pool.

I am targeting five measured zero-value outlets with saleable concentrates: the C6 naphthene-rich BTBB, cyclohexane-rich BBTTTT, and three small but easily split C4/C5 and C7/C8 streams. These additions should convert stranded material into revenue while keeping the proven convergent base flowsheet.

The current measured leaves contain recoverable propane, butane/isopentane, cyclohexane, and methylcyclopentane. I am adding small polishing columns on those zero-value leaves, with a much sharper column only for the close hexane/methylcyclopentane cut.

Three existing 95–97% pure products are just below premium grade. Small polishing columns should remove their light/heavy impurities and capture the 20% price uplift, especially the roughly $90M/yr upside on the large octane stream.

The measured BBBT feed is already 97% n-octane and therefore saleable, while its column destroys value by producing one unsold outlet and a smaller pure outlet. Selling it directly should recover about $154M/yr of revenue and eliminate $16.5M/yr of column cost.

The measured BTBBTT stream still loses about 33 mol/s methylcyclopentane with hexane, while two small C3/C4/C5 tails also remain unsold. I am testing sharper final splits; the large BTBBT column uses the already-convergent high-severity, deep-pressure-drop pattern of BTB.

The current 32-column flowsheet is valid but less profitable than the stored best (3.293 versus 3.357). I am restoring the best measured design before using the remaining solves on targeted cost reductions.

Use the remaining budget on purity upgrades with direct revenue upside: premium octane and isopentane, recovery of unsold light ends, and a lower-boilup hexane/MCP cut to avoid sending excessive MCP overhead. These are targeted hypotheses; the measured baseline is reward 3.357 with several 95–97% products and small unsold outlets.

Remove the nonconvergent, zero-value propane/isobutane column to restore validity. Use the final two solves to reduce BTBBT boil-up so its distillate approaches saleable n-hexane while retaining pure methylcyclopentane bottoms, and increase TTBBTB boil-up to recover saleable isopentane bottoms; both streams currently have measurable unsold value.
